strengths: The core idea is simple and practical: use the implicit token-level reward defined by the DPO/SFT log-ratio (as motivated by Rafailov et al., 2024b's Q-function interpretation) directly as a decoding-time objective, requiring no extra training or auxiliary models beyond the standard DPO pipeline.

Broad and reasonably systematic empirical evaluation: six preference datasets, four model/scale combinations (Llama 3B/8B, Qwen 0.6B/4B), and comparisons against greedy SFT/DPO, best-of-2, and an EFT variant, plus an external AlpacaEval evaluation.

Several useful auxiliary studies beyond the main comparison: robustness to the DPO regularization parameter β (Fig. 4), performance under data scarcity (Fig. 3), a BoN-vs-AAD compute-matched comparison (Fig. 2), an entropy-thresholding fix for beam-search collapse (Fig. 6), and an iterative-DPO pipeline that uses AAD-generated completions as high-quality synthetic preference data to close the gap to full-data training (Fig. 5).

The paper offers a clear (if simple) theoretical argument for why the exact optimal DPO policy π* can still favor a lower-reward completion because it inherits πSFT's biases (Eq. 6), motivating why re-introducing the SFT model at inference time is useful.
Qualitative examples (Figs. 1, 8-11) are provided that illustrate token-level behavior of AAD versus greedy/BoN decoding, aiding interpretability.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: AAD's token score (Eq. 7) is mathematically identical to the implicit token-level reward already used in emulated fine-tuning/contrastive-decoding-style methods (Mitchell et al. 2024; Li et al. 2023a), applied here to the same model's own SFT/DPO checkpoints rather than a separate base/aligned pair, plus min-α token filtering borrowed from min-p sampling (Minh et al. 2025). The paper does not clearly disentangle how much of the improvement over the EFT baseline comes from this self-referential setup versus the α-filtering mechanism, since the EFT baseline as configured (πSFT as both base and reference, β=4) is confusingly close to unfiltered AAD; no ablation isolates the filtering contribution on greedy decoding.

Reproducibility gap: Section A.6 promises a codebase link ("the source code associated with this study can be accessed at:") but no URL is actually provided in the manuscript, undermining the stated reproducibility support.

Presentation issues suggest incomplete editing: the related-work section ends mid-sentence ("These approaches typically"), and dense result tables lack any variance/confidence intervals or statistical significance testing across the many close numeric comparisons (e.g., R and W values that differ by small margins).

The BoN comparison (Fig. 2) shows AAD's advantage narrows or is matched by BoN at moderate N on Skywork, and computational cost claims ("efficiency comparable to standard decoding") are inconsistent with the method's actual requirement of two forward passes per token plus keeping the SFT model resident in memory, a real overhead only briefly acknowledged in the conclusion.

The iterative-DPO and beam-search stabilization experiments are conducted on a single model/dataset combination each (Llama3.2-3B on Skywork), limiting confidence that these secondary findings generalize across the broader set of models/datasets used in the main table.

The theoretical contribution (bias inheritance argument, Eq. 6) is a relatively straightforward restatement of known results (DPO not training a reward-maximizing policy, per Rafailov et al. 2024b) rather than a substantially new theoretical insight.

strengths: The core idea—using the log-ratio between the DPO-trained policy and its SFT reference as an implicit token-level reward for greedy decoding—is well motivated by the Q-function interpretation of DPO (Rafailov et al., 2024b) and is simple to implement without extra training or auxiliary reward models.

The empirical evaluation is broad: six preference datasets, two model families (Llama, Qwen) at multiple scales, both LoRA and full fine-tuning settings, and an external AlpacaEval evaluation, consistently showing gains over greedy decoding and best-of-2.

Several useful ablations are included: robustness to the DPO regularization parameter β, behavior under data scarcity (varying training set size), a BoN compute-matched comparison, and a demonstration that AAD-generated completions can bootstrap iterative DPO under limited labeled data.

The min-α token filtering and entropy-thresholded beam search extensions show the authors anticipated and partially addressed degenerate/over-optimized completions, which is a known failure mode of reward-guided decoding.
weaknesses: Novelty is thin relative to prior inference-time alignment work explicitly discussed in Section 2 (EFT, DeRa, ARGS, controlled decoding, GenARM, weak-to-strong search): AAD is essentially a same-scale variant of emulated fine-tuning/contrastive decoding using the (πSFT, πDPO) pair, and the paper does not empirically compare against the most directly related methods (ARGS, controlled decoding, GenARM, weak-to-strong search, IVG) despite extensive discussion of them, undermining claims of consistent superiority over 'strong baselines.'

The EFT baseline appears to be configured in a way (πSFT used as both base and reference, fixed β=4) that is not a faithful or clearly justified reproduction of the original EFT setup, raising concern about whether the comparison is fair; no ablation or citation justifies this specific configuration as EFT's best setting other than an unsupported claim.

Evaluation relies entirely on reward models trained by the authors (pickers/oracles) with modest reported accuracies (e.g., 62–70% for HHRLHF/Ultrachat in Table 3) and on AlpacaEval with an unspecified 'default evaluator'; no human evaluation is conducted, so the central alignment claims rest on potentially noisy, self-trained proxy metrics rather than independently validated preference signals.

No variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for any of the many reward/win-rate numbers in Table 1, 2, and 4, making it hard to judge whether the reported gains are robust versus noise, especially for smaller differences (e.g., Qwen 0.6B Nectar 1.68 vs EFT 1.23).

The method's computational cost (two forward passes per token, requiring both πDPO and πSFT in memory) is acknowledged only briefly as a limitation without concrete wall-clock/throughput comparisons against baselines of ostensibly 'comparable' cost (Bo2, EFT), despite this being central to the practicality of an inference-time method.

Reproducibility is undermined by an appendix that promises source code ('the source code... can be accessed at:') but provides no actual link, and by an apparent typo/error in Eq. (5), where the denominator is written as 'log πSFT(y|x)' instead of 'πSFT(y|x)', creating an inconsistency in a key derivation.

The qualitative examples (Fig. 1, 8-11) are presented as evidence of AAD's superiority but are subjective, small in number, and not backed by any quantitative human annotation, so their persuasive value is limited.

The paper text itself contains an unfinished sentence at the end of Section 2 ('These approaches typically') and other presentation issues, suggesting the manuscript was not thoroughly proofread before submission.

The choice of hyperparameters (α=0.1 for main experiments vs. α=0.7 for beam-search stabilization, β=4 for EFT, β=0.1 default for DPO training) is not systematically justified or ablated in a unified way, leaving open how sensitive the method's reported advantage is to these choices.

strengths: The method is simple and practical: it reuses artifacts that are already produced by standard DPO training (the DPO-aligned model and its SFT reference) without requiring any additional training, auxiliary reward models, or hyperparameter search beyond a single filtering threshold.

The theoretical motivation is clear and grounded in prior work (Rafailov et al. 2024b's Q-function interpretation of DPO); Section 4's derivation showing that the analytically optimal DPO policy can still prefer a lower-reward completion over a higher-reward one is a nice, intuitive justification for why using the likelihood ratio directly at decoding time can help.

The empirical evaluation is broad: six preference datasets, four model variants (Llama 3B/8B, Qwen 0.6B/4B) with LoRA alignment, plus an additional full fine-tuning ablation on Llama 1B/3B, and an external AlpacaEval evaluation — consistent gains are shown across almost all settings.

Several thoughtful ablations strengthen the paper's claims: robustness to the DPO regularization parameter β, performance under data scarcity, comparison against Best-of-N with oracle/picker rankers at matched compute, entropy-thresholded beam search to avoid beam collapse, and an iterative-DPO pipeline showing AAD-generated synthetic data can substitute for real preference data.
Qualitative examples (Figs. 1, 8–11) are illustrative and provide some intuition for how AAD differs from greedy/Bo2 decoding in realistic generation scenarios.
weaknesses: The core technical idea is conceptually close to several existing inference-time alignment methods discussed in the related work (EFT, DeRa, contrastive decoding with min-p/min-alpha filtering), amounting mainly to applying the implicit DPO reward with the *same* aligned/reference pair at decoding time rather than transferring it across models; the incremental nature of this contribution relative to Liu et al. (2024d, DeRa), which already explores decoding-time use of the DPO log-ratio, is not clearly disentangled.

The paper explicitly identifies ARGS, controlled decoding, DeAl, reward-guided beam search, weak-to-strong decoding, and IVG as closest related work, but none of these are included as empirical baselines — only Greedy SFT/DPO, Best-of-2, and one EFT variant are compared, leaving open whether AAD's gains hold against the most directly comparable explicit/implicit-reward search methods.

All evaluation relies on learned reward models (oracle/picker, or off-the-shelf reward models for Skywork/Nectar) rather than any human evaluation; since AAD is explicitly framed as optimizing an implicit reward signal, favorable scores under reward-model-based oracles could partly reflect reward-model artifacts/overlap rather than genuine alignment improvement, and this risk is not directly investigated (e.g., via human studies or diversity/degeneracy checks).

Reported computational costs are only loosely compared (AAD needs two forward passes per token, similar to EFT/Bo2, while greedy baselines need one), but no wall-clock or FLOP-normalized comparison is given, and AAD's own win-rate column is trivially omitted as the reference method, making some rows (e.g., Table 1) slightly harder to interpret as an independent apples-to-apples comparison.

The method's practical robustness depends on at least two additional hyperparameters (α for token filtering, τ for entropy thresholding in the beam-search extension) that appear to require per-dataset/per-setting tuning (e.g., α=0.1 for greedy AAD vs. α=0.7 for the beam-search experiment), which somewhat undercuts the simplicity claim.

All experiments are limited to relatively small models (≤8B parameters); it remains unclear how AAD behaves at larger scales or with more modern alignment methods beyond vanilla DPO (e.g., KTO, IPO), limiting confidence in the generality of the significance claims.

There are minor presentation issues, e.g., an incomplete sentence at the end of Section 2 ("These approaches typically"), which suggests the manuscript could benefit from a more careful proofreading pass.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical evaluation: 6 preference datasets, 4 model families/scales (Llama 3B/8B, Qwen 0.6B/4B), plus additional experiments on OLMo-2 7B/13B open-source DPO models, giving good evidence of generalization across architectures and scales.

Multiple independent evaluation protocols (in-house oracle reward models, external off-the-shelf reward models for Skywork/Nectar, AlpacaEval with GPT-4/GPT-4-turbo judges, and a genuine human study with 502 pairwise judgments/40 raters) consistently support the paper's central claim, which mitigates concerns about reward-model gaming of a single oracle.

Reasonable theoretical motivation grounding the method in the Q-function/token-level MDP interpretation of DPO (Rafailov et al., 2024b), with a full derivation in the appendix explaining why the aligned policy can favor lower-reward completions and why the log-ratio can serve as a token-level advantage.

Careful and honest ablations: effect of the filtering threshold α, robustness to DPO's β regularization parameter, behavior under full fine-tuning vs LoRA, data-scarcity scaling (both LoRA and full fine-tuning), beam search interactions (including failure modes like beam collapse), and a forthright negative/mixed result when combining AAD with PPO-trained (rather than DPO-trained) policies.

The iterative-DPO application (using AAD-generated synthetic data to retrain via DPO) is a genuinely useful downstream contribution for data-scarce settings, supported by experiments on multiple datasets showing near-parity with full-data training using only 10% of labeled preference data.
Fixed hyperparameter (α = 0.1) transfers across all 6 datasets and 4 model families without per-task tuning, supporting practical usability.
weaknesses: The core method is conceptually very close to existing inference-time alignment techniques, particularly emulated fine-tuning (EFT, Mitchell et al. 2024) and contrastive decoding (Li et al., 2023b): AAD is essentially contrastive decoding applied to a DPO/SFT model pair with min-α plausibility filtering drawn from the DPO model rather than a generic amateur model. The distinction from EFT (argmax over a token-level ratio vs. reweighted sampling from a combined distribution) is somewhat subtle, and the paper's differentiation from these closely related methods could be argued more rigorously rather than largely through the ablation in Table 3.

The theoretical justification (Appendix A.1) shows that log π*/πSFT relates to a KL-shaped instantaneous reward plus a difference of value functions, but does not rigorously establish that greedy token-level maximization of this ratio yields better *sequence-level* reward than sampling from π* itself; the argument that AAD is 'more direct' is intuitive rather than proven, and the myopic (non-lookahead) nature of greedy decoding is a known limitation only partially addressed via the beam-search ablation.

No variance/confidence intervals are reported for the main results in Table 1 and Table 2 (only Figure 3 and Figure 9 show variability across datasets), making it hard to assess the statistical significance of reported gains, especially for smaller models (e.g., Qwen 0.6B) where reward values are close to zero.

The oracle-reward-based evaluation, while partially validated with external reward models and human studies, still relies heavily on learned reward models trained on the same or related data distributions in most experiments (4 of 6 datasets), leaving residual risk of reward-model bias/overoptimization influencing the main quantitative claims in Table 1.

AAD requires access to both the DPO-aligned and the original SFT reference model at inference (2x forward passes), which is a genuine practical constraint the paper acknowledges but that materially limits applicability to settings where only the aligned model is available (e.g., many deployed/open-weight releases without a paired SFT checkpoint).

The method's inconsistency when applied to PPO-trained policies (Table 10) suggests the 'standard DPO setup' requirement is a real limitation rather than a minor caveat, since much production alignment still uses RLHF/PPO pipelines; this narrows the claimed scope of applicability to models trained specifically via SFT+DPO, and details on why AAD sometimes underperforms with PPO models are relatively brief.

Code repository link is left blank in the manuscript (placeholder text 'Code available at' / 'source code associated with this study can be accessed at:'), so reproducibility currently rests entirely on the appendix's hyperparameter tables rather than a verifiable implementation.

strengths: The method is simple and practical: it reuses the SFT and DPO checkpoints that are already produced by a standard preference-optimization pipeline, requiring no additional training, reward model, or external smaller model.

The empirical evaluation is broad in scope, spanning six preference datasets (Ultrafeedback, Argilla, OpenRLHF Mixture, HHRLHF, Nectar, Skywork), multiple model families and scales (Llama 3B/8B/1B, Qwen 0.6B/4B, OLMo-2-7B/13B), LoRA and full fine-tuning, and several evaluation protocols (oracle reward models, AlpacaEval with GPT-4, and a human preference study).

A reasonably large set of ablations is provided (effect of alpha and beta, data scarcity, beam search stabilization via entropy thresholding, training epoch/overtraining effects, comparison to contrastive decoding with weak reference models), which helps characterize when and why the method works.

The paper is candid about some limitations, e.g., the 2x inference cost, dependency on access to the SFT checkpoint, and the negative/mixed result when combining AAD with PPO-trained policies (Table 10), rather than hiding this failure case.
The iterative-DPO extension (using AAD-generated completions as synthetic preference data) is a useful practical application for low-resource settings and is tested on multiple datasets.
weaknesses: Originality is limited: the core mechanism (log-ratio between an aligned and a reference/base model used as a token-level signal, combined with top-p/min-alpha style filtering) is very close to already-cited prior work, particularly contrastive decoding, emulated fine-tuning (EFT), DeRa, and weak-to-strong search/decoding. The paper's own related-work section lists numerous methods that already use reference-aligned model pairs for implicit token-level rewards; the delta here (using the model's own SFT/DPO pair with min-alpha filtering instead of an external pair) is incremental rather than conceptually new.

The theoretical justification in Section 4 and Appendix A.1 derives the optimal ratio log π*(a|s)/πSFT(a|s) assuming access to the *exact* optimal policy π*, but the method substitutes the empirically trained πDPO (which the paper itself argues is a biased, finite-sample approximation of π*). There is no rigorous argument or proof that greedy argmax decoding on this empirical ratio recovers a policy with higher true reward than sampling from πDPO itself; the connection between the single-token advantage A(v) and maximization of the full-sequence human-aligned reward rH is asserted by analogy rather than established formally.

Evaluation relies heavily on reward models trained on the same data distribution (oracle and picker RMs), which the paper's own introduction acknowledges can be exploited/gamed (citing reward-model over-optimization literature); only a subset of settings (Skywork/Nectar/OLMo) use external RMs or human/GPT-4 judges, and the human study covers only one model/dataset combination (3B Llama on Skywork, 502 judgments), which is a fairly narrow basis for the strong overall claims made in the abstract.

The claim that AAD remains competitive with, or even surpasses, Best-of-N sampling using an oracle RM for large N (Figure 2) is striking and somewhat counterintuitive—since BoN with the oracle directly optimizes the evaluation metric—but is not critically examined; this raises the possibility that the oracle-reward evaluation itself has exploitable biases (e.g., length or stylistic artifacts) that AAD may be exploiting more effectively than full-sequence resampling, rather than genuinely producing superior generations.

Efficiency claims are overstated in places: the conclusion states AAD maintains 'efficiency comparable to standard decoding,' but the method requires two forward passes per token and the paper's own appendix reports throughput as low as 0.5x–0.75x relative to greedy decoding, comparable to EFT and Bo2 rather than to standard single-model decoding.

Hyperparameter robustness claims (e.g., that alpha=0.1 'transfers across tasks and model scales without per-dataset tuning') are based on an ablation using only one model scale (3B Llama) across three datasets (Figure 3), which is a limited basis for such a general claim.

Many of the qualitative examples (Figures 1, 11–14) are presented as evidence of AAD's superior 'helpfulness' or 'prompt adherence,' but these are single cherry-picked anecdotes evaluated subjectively by the authors rather than through a systematic qualitative protocol, weakening their evidentiary value.

The paper reports point estimates throughout the main tables (Table 1, 2, 4, etc.) without confidence intervals or statistical significance testing, making it difficult to assess whether some of the smaller reported gaps (e.g., some HHRLHF or Nectar results) are meaningful.

strengths: The core idea—using the log-ratio between the DPO-aligned model and its SFT reference as a token-level advantage/reward signal for decoding—is theoretically grounded via the token-level MDP / Q-function interpretation of DPO (building on Rafailov et al. 2024b), and the derivation is spelled out in detail in Appendix A.1.

Very extensive empirical validation: 6 preference datasets, 4 model families/scales (Llama 3B/8B, Qwen 0.6B/4B), external (held-out) oracle reward models for Skywork/Nectar to reduce evaluation circularity, AlpacaEval (GPT-4 judge) results, open-source OLMo-2-7B/13B DPO checkpoints, and an actual human evaluation study (502 pairwise judgments, 40 raters) that corroborates the automatic metrics.

Thorough ablations: effect of the filtering threshold α, robustness to DPO's β regularization, data-scarcity scaling curves (LoRA and full fine-tuning), beam search with entropy thresholding, overtraining analysis, and direct comparison to related inference-time methods (EFT, Bo2, contrastive decoding with weaker amateur models).

A useful and somewhat novel secondary contribution: using AAD-generated completions as synthetic preference data for iterative DPO, which nearly closes the gap to full-data training when only 10% of labeled preference data is available—practically relevant for data-constrained alignment.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper explicitly reports a negative/mixed result when combining AAD with PPO-trained policies (Table 10) rather than hiding it, and acknowledges the 2x forward-pass inference cost and dependence on having the SFT checkpoint.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: AAD is essentially a specific instantiation of the EFT/contrastive-decoding family (token-level log-ratio between an aligned and a reference/amateur model, with probability-mass filtering reminiscent of Li et al. 2023b's contrastive decoding). While the paper differentiates AAD from EFT and CD empirically (Table 3), the conceptual distance from prior work is relatively small.

No direct empirical comparison against several inference-time alignment baselines discussed in related work (ARGS, controlled decoding, DeRa, weak-to-strong search, GenARM, Amulet), leaving open how AAD compares to the broader field of more sophisticated search/guided-decoding methods, not just the four selected baselines.

The reward/oracle evaluation for four of six datasets relies on reward models trained on the same data distribution as the picker/DPO models, which can inflate apparent gains despite the 90/10 split; the external-oracle experiments (Skywork, Nectar) partially but not fully address this concern for the rest of the benchmarks.

The paper states 'Code available at' with no actual link filled in anywhere in the main text or appendix (Section A.5), which is a reproducibility gap for a paper whose contribution is largely empirical/engineering in nature.

The reported gains are reward-model-driven; there is no analysis of potential confounds such as response length or verbosity bias in the reward models, which is a well-known issue in RLHF/DPO evaluation, and the qualitative examples (Figures 1, 11–14) show AAD often producing longer, more elaborate answers, raising the question of whether some of the improvement is a length/verbosity artifact rather than genuine alignment quality.

The human evaluation, while a valuable addition, is limited to a single model size (3B Llama) and a single dataset (Skywork), making it unclear whether the human-judged advantage generalizes across the many other settings reported with automatic metrics.

The α threshold, while claimed to transfer well, is only explicitly ablated on one model (3B Llama) across three datasets (Figure 3); broader sensitivity analysis across model scales would strengthen the claim of hyperparameter-free deployment.

Practical overhead (two forward passes per token, ~0.5-0.75x throughput relative to greedy decoding) is non-trivial and could limit adoption compared to single-pass decoding baselines, which is acknowledged but not deeply mitigated.
